title: Reforming the Judiciary -- Ch. 11: Saving the Constitutional System
keywords: imploring the aid of Almighty God
theist, not atheist, not even agnostic
confluence of events planned in heaven
primary_topics: Chapter 11 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- a symposium address at the UST Central Seminary in which CJP opened with the Centennial Prayer for the Court, defended its constitutionality, and then gave a first-hand account of the Supreme Court's role in the ascendancy of Gloria Macapagal Arroyo to the Presidency.

He argued that an official court prayer does not violate the separation of church and state, because the doctrine requires only government neutrality among religious denominations, and because the Philippines is monotheist and its Constitution itself begins by imploring the aid of Almighty God -- so that while there is separation of church and state, there is no separation of the state from God.

He narrated the events of January 16-20, 2001: the Senate Impeachment Court's 11-10 refusal to open the second envelope, the EDSA throng, the resignations, the withdrawal of military and police support, his conclusion that there was no effectively functioning government, and his 5:30 a.m. call proposing that Chief Justice Davide swear in Vice President Arroyo by noon.

He then set out the Court's legal aftermath -- the January 22, 2001 Resolution confirming the Chief Justice's authority, the unanimous 13-0 decision in Estrada v. Desierto and Estrada v. Arroyo, and the four distinct theories (resignation, permanent disability, abandonment and reality) by which the justices reached that common conclusion -- and closed with an epilogue reading EDSA 2 as the work of the Holy Spirit.
sub_topics: The Centennial Prayer for the Court, recited at the start of each Supreme Court session and authorized for all courts, composed the previous year by the Centenary Execom he chairs after repeated consultation with Catholic, Protestant, Muslim, Born-again and other religious groups.

The separation-of-church-and-state objection answered: the Philippines is theist, not atheist, not even agnostic, indeed monotheist, and the Constitution begins 'We, the sovereign Filipino people, imploring the aid of Almighty God'; both houses of Congress and the Cabinet also preface sessions with prayers.

What the doctrine actually forbids: appropriating or spending public funds for one denomination's basilica, promoting one group's tenets to the detriment of others, paying priests or imams for strictly religious duties, and using religion as a condition for any right or privilege.

The invitation from Fr. Honorato C. Castigador, OP and Seminarian Francis A. Tordila and their congratulations on his statesmanship, which he deflected in Filipino -- he had only done his duty as a Filipino.

The occasion for the topic: the Philippine Daily Inquirer's naming of the Supreme Court as 'Filipino of the Year 2001' for saving the constitutional system from collapse, with a poll majority approving and a minority holding the Court to be on the wrong side of history -- a charge he declined to answer, leaving history as the ultimate judge.

The spark of EDSA 2: the 11-10 vote of the Senate Impeachment Court refusing to open the second envelope said to contain evidence linking President Estrada to the multimillion 'Jose Velarde' deposit in Equitable-PCI Bank.

The cascade: the chanting throng at the EDSA Shrine, resignations by Cabinet members and high officials, religious, civic, business, professional and NGO groups chorusing 'Erap, resign,' and a united print, radio and TV press.

The decisive afternoon of Friday, January 19, 2001, when all the heads of the major commands of the AFP and the PNP withdrew support from Estrada and pledged allegiance to Vice President Arroyo, leaving Estrada unable to govern and Arroyo unable to lead legally.

His sleepless night and 4:00 a.m. television watch on January 20, when Cardinal Sin, through Msgr. Socrates Villegas, pleaded with the rallyists not to march to Mendiola where pro-Erap partisans were encamped, Fr. Robert Keyes supported the plea, and militant leaders announced they would march at 6:00 a.m. unless Estrada resigned.

The grim scenario he foresaw: violence and bloodshed if the two groups clashed, a revolutionary government if Mrs. Arroyo acted while a legally recognized President remained, or a coup d'etat -- in any case the obliteration of the Constitution, the abolition of constitutional offices, economic collapse and civil strife.

His conclusion after prayer and reflection that the only way to avert bloodshed and save the democratic system was to have Mrs. Arroyo sworn in, and his 5:30 a.m. call to Chief Justice Davide proposing the oath by noon.

Why only the Supreme Court could act: the Court and its members are normally passive officials who act on petitions, but the situation was extraordinary, only the Court had the credibility and moral authority to avert catastrophe, and Davide's performance as presiding officer of the impeachment court had made him the most trusted Filipino in a scientific poll.

Davide's immediate agreement, CJP's announcement over radio and television, a questioning call from another justice, and the emergency session at which all twelve justices present backed the swearing in provided GMA made a formal written request -- after which they went to the EDSA Shrine to witness it.

The legal aftermath: the January 22, 2001 Resolution confirming the Chief Justice's authority to swear in GMA as President; the March 2, 2001 unanimous 13-0 Decision in Estrada v. Desierto and Estrada v. Arroyo upholding her legitimacy, with Davide and CJP inhibiting themselves because of their participation; and the 13-0 denial with finality of Estrada's Motion for Reconsideration on April 3, 2001.
His voluntary recusal: prepared to submit his own written opinion, he yielded to Estrada's request and recused himself, hoping to present his own view at the proper time.

Article VII, Section 8 of the Constitution on succession, and the four theories: Resignation, drawn from 'the totality of prior, contemporaneous and posterior facts and circumstantial evidence' despite the absence of a written resignation; Permanent Disability, read by Justice Bellosillo to cover functional and not merely physical or mental incapacity, and by Justice Mendoza as a vacuum in executive leadership; Abandonment, per Justice Vitug, as giving up the office without the formalities of resignation; and the Reality Theory of four magistrates, in Justice Gutierrez's words that the Court 'has to declare as a fact what in fact exists.'

Chief Justice Davide's Foreword to 'A Centenary of Justice,' calling the unanimous Decision a watershed event cast in concrete at the portals of constitutionalism and saying that the two recusals strengthened judicial independence and the rule of law.

The epilogue of faith: his continuing wonder at how he summoned the courage to propose the oath before GMA requested it and while Estrada was still in Malacañang, and why Davide agreed before consulting the other justices -- explicable only as the work of the Holy Spirit.

The two men's Scripture habits -- CJP taking his bearings from the daily Mass readings, Davide cutting the Bible and reflecting on the page that opens -- and Davide's 3:30 a.m. reading on January 20 of Isaiah 62, the Restoration of Zion, which struck him as a call to restore normalcy to the country.

The gospel of January 20, 2001, Mark 3:20-21, in which the Lord was accused by his own relatives of being out of his mind and by the scribes of being possessed -- a warning that those who espouse unorthodox ideas may be thought insane, and that one should stand fast when the eccentricity is born of faith.

stances.claim: The Supreme Court's official prayer does not violate the separation of church and state, because the doctrine requires only that government be neutral in the competition among religious denominations -- and while there is separation of church and state, there is no separation of the state from God.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal narrowing plus textual proof: enumerating what the clause actually forbids, then citing the Constitution's own opening invocation and the practice of Congress and the Cabinet

stances.claim: From the afternoon of January 19, 2001, when the AFP and PNP commands withdrew their support, Estrada could not effectively govern and Arroyo could not legally lead, so that there was no effectively functioning government in the country.
stances.rhetorical_move: first-hand situational diagnosis, dated and sourced to the events he watched unfold

stances.claim: The only way to avert violence, chaos and bloodshed and to save the democratic system from collapse was to have Mrs. Arroyo sworn in as President, since every alternative -- a clash at Mendiola, a revolutionary government, or a coup d'etat -- would have obliterated the Constitution and abolished the constitutional offices.
stances.rhetorical_move: elimination of alternatives: laying out the grim scenario branch by branch until one course remains

stances.claim: Although the Supreme Court and its members are normally passive officials who act only on a proper petition, the country faced an extraordinary situation that demanded an extraordinary solution, and only the Court -- and only Chief Justice Davide, whom a poll had made the most trusted Filipino -- had the credibility and moral authority to avert a governmental catastrophe.
stances.rhetorical_move: exception-to-passivity argument grounded in institutional credibility rather than in jurisdiction

stances.claim: The Court was unanimous that Arroyo was the legitimate, constitutional and permanent President and that Estrada was no longer Chief Executive, but the justices were not united in their reasons, which fall into four theories: resignation, permanent disability, abandonment and reality.
stances.rhetorical_move: taxonomy of a divided rationale behind a unanimous result, each theory attributed to named justices and quoted

stances.claim: EDSA 2 was a confluence of events planned in heaven, and the Court's extraordinary action can only be explained as the work of the Holy Spirit -- on him, on Chief Justice Davide, whose Bible opened that morning to Isaiah 62 on the Restoration of Zion, and on all the key players.
stances.rhetorical_move: providential reading of a constitutional crisis, corroborated by the two men's Scripture habits and the day's gospel reading

notable_anecdotes: He began by asking the audience to rise while he recited the Centennial Prayer for the Court, then explained that the justices take turns leading it at each session and that the Court has authorized its recitation in all courts nationwide.
Thanked by his hosts for his statesmanship during the crucial political events of the Republic, he answered in Filipino that he had only done his duty as a Filipino.

Unable to rest on the night of January 19, he fell asleep about 1:00 a.m., woke at 4:00 a.m. and switched on the bedroom television, where he heard that Cardinal Sin, through Msgr. Socrates Villegas, was pleading with the EDSA rallyists not to march on Mendiola, while militant leaders vowed to march at 6:00 a.m. unless Estrada resigned.

After prayer and reflection he summoned the courage to telephone Chief Justice Davide at about 5:30 a.m. and propose that, to save the Constitution, Davide swear in Gloria Macapagal Arroyo by noon that day.

When a justice heard the radio and television announcement and telephoned the Court to question the proposal, Davide called all the members to an emergency session, where after animated discussion the twelve justices present -- three were out of town -- backed the swearing in on condition that GMA submit a formal written request, and then went to the EDSA Shrine to witness the oath.

He revealed that he had been prepared to submit his own written opinion in the Estrada cases but yielded to Estrada's request and recused himself voluntarily, hoping to present his own view at the proper time.

He recounted Davide's habit of cutting the Bible and reflecting on the page that opens: on the morning of January 20, after waking as usual at 3:30 a.m., Davide's Bible fell open to Isaiah 62, the 'Restoration of Zion,' which struck him as a call to restore normalcy -- so that by 5:30 a.m. he was already ready for what CJP calls his 'weird-sounding' proposal.

He noted that the gospel for January 20, 2001 was Mark 3:20-21, where the Lord's own relatives said he was out of his mind and the scribes said he was possessed -- a parallel he drew to those who espouse unorthodox ideas.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduced a symposium address at the University of Sto. Tomas Central Seminary. Justice Panganiban opened by having the audience rise for the Centennial Prayer for the Court, composed by the Centenary Executive Committee he chaired after consultations with Catholic, Protestant, Muslim, Born-again and other groups, and now recited at each Supreme Court session and in all courts. Answering the objection that an official prayer breaches the separation of church and state, he argued that the Philippines is theist, not atheist, not even agnostic, that the Constitution itself opens by imploring the aid of Almighty God, and that the doctrine requires only government neutrality among denominations -- forbidding public funds for one group's basilica, promotion of one group's tenets, salaries for religious duties, or religion as a condition of any right -- so that while there is separation of church and state, there is no separation of the state from God. Turning to the topic he had been given, and to the Inquirer's naming of the Court as 'Filipino of the Year 2001,' he recounted January 16-20, 2001: the Senate Impeachment Court's 11-10 refusal to open the second envelope said to link President Estrada to the 'Jose Velarde' deposit, the EDSA throng, mass resignations, and the withdrawal of AFP and PNP support on the afternoon of January 19, after which, he concluded, there was no effectively functioning government. Sleepless, he woke at 4:00 a.m., heard that militants would march on Mendiola by six, foresaw bloodshed, a revolutionary government or a coup -- each obliterating the Constitution -- and at 5:30 a.m. telephoned Chief Justice Davide to propose that he swear in Vice President Arroyo by noon. Davide agreed at once; an emergency session of the twelve justices present endorsed it subject to a written request. He then traced the aftermath: the January 22 Resolution, the 13-0 Decision of March 2, 2001 in Estrada v. Desierto and Estrada v. Arroyo with his and Davide's recusals, the 13-0 denial of reconsideration, and the four theories -- resignation, permanent disability, abandonment and reality -- behind the unanimous result. He closed by reading EDSA 2 as a confluence of events planned in heaven, citing Davide's Bible falling open to Isaiah 62 and the day's gospel from Mark.
